Gender scoring and the census name table

Source: vignettes/gender-scoring.Rmd
gender-scoring.Rmd

Every parse returns a gender code (M, F or U) and a gender_confidence. Both are estimates from how often the given names are recorded for men and for women in U.S. Census name lists. This article shows how the score is computed, what the confidence means, when the parser falls back to a default, and where the census table comes from.

The score

determine_gender() takes the census rows for the given-name tokens (the first name and any middle names, never the surname), adds up their male and female counts, and reports the larger side:

confidence=100×max(nmale,nfemale)nmale+nfemale \text{confidence} = 100 \times \frac{\max(n_{male},\, n_{female})}{n_{male} + n_{female}}

rounded to one decimal place.

cd <- get_census_data(c("LESLIE"))
cd[, c("name", "male_value", "female_value")]
#>      name male_value female_value
#>    <char>      <num>        <num>
#> 1: LESLIE      52838       237654
determine_gender(cd)
#> [1] "F"    "81.8"

The confidence is the share of people with these names who have the reported gender. It runs from 50 (an even split) to 100 (only one gender recorded). It is not the probability that this particular person has that gender, which also depends on their age and on the population the record comes from.

show(c("JOHN SMITH", "MARY SMITH", "LESLIE SMITH", "PAT SMITH",
       "CHRIS JONES", "TAYLOR SWIFT"))
#>            raw salutation first_name middle_name suffix gender gender_confidence
#> 1   JOHN SMITH                  JOHN                         M              99.8
#> 2   MARY SMITH                  MARY                         F              99.8
#> 3 LESLIE SMITH                LESLIE                         F              81.8
#> 4    PAT SMITH                   PAT                         F              59.5
#> 5  CHRIS JONES                 CHRIS                         M              94.4
#> 6 TAYLOR SWIFT                TAYLOR                         F              75.5

Most first names in the table are strongly gendered. Of the 53616 first names, the majority gender holds 95% or more of the count for most of them:

fn <- census.names[census.names$first_name_value > 0, ]
share <- pmax(fn$male_value, fn$female_value) / (fn$male_value + fn$female_value)
table(cut(share, c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95, 1), include.lowest = TRUE,
          labels = c("50-80%", "80-95%", "95-100%")))
#> 
#>  50-80%  80-95% 95-100% 
#>    7454    9093   37069

Middle names count too

The counts of all given-name tokens are pooled, so the middle name can move the score. Because the counts are pooled rather than averaged, a very common name outweighs a rare one, and two names of opposite gender give a weak score whatever their order:

show(c("SARAH MAY WILSON", "JOHN MARY SMITH", "MARY JOHN SMITH"))
#>                raw salutation first_name middle_name suffix gender gender_confidence
#> 1 SARAH MAY WILSON                 SARAH         MAY             F              99.8
#> 2  JOHN MARY SMITH                  JOHN        MARY             M              63.8
#> 3  MARY JOHN SMITH                  MARY        JOHN             M              63.8

When there is no evidence

When no given-name token is in the census (an initial, a rare name, or no given name at all), the parser falls back:

Situation gender gender_confidence
given names not in the census, no suffix U 50.0
given names not in the census, with JR, SR, II, … M 50.0
nothing left to parse U 0.0

The suffix rule reflects that generational suffixes are almost always used by men. The 50.0 says that the call is a default, not evidence.

show(c("J SMITH", "J SMITH JR", "A J SMITH", "TSHEPO CHO", "SMITH JR"))
#>          raw salutation first_name middle_name suffix gender gender_confidence
#> 1    J SMITH                     J                         U              50.0
#> 2 J SMITH JR                     J                 JR      M              50.0
#> 3  A J SMITH                     A           J             U              50.0
#> 4 TSHEPO CHO                TSHEPO                         U              50.0
#> 5   SMITH JR                                       JR      M              50.0

Salutations

parse_name() does not use the salutation for gender: MR PAT SMITH is scored from PAT alone. If you need a salutation to override the census score, do it after parsing:

d <- show(c("MR PAT SMITH", "MRS PAT SMITH", "DR PAT SMITH"))
d$gender_sal <- ifelse(d$salutation == "MR", "M",
                ifelse(d$salutation %in% c("MRS", "MS", "MISS"), "F", d$gender))
d
#>             raw salutation first_name middle_name suffix gender gender_confidence gender_sal
#> 1  MR PAT SMITH         MR        PAT                         F              59.5          M
#> 2 MRS PAT SMITH        MRS        PAT                         F              59.5          F
#> 3  DR PAT SMITH         DR        PAT                         F              59.5          F

The nickname functions do this already: in nickname_lookup() a gendered salutation (MR, MRS, MS, MISS) beats the census score. See vignette("canonical-first-names").

Using the scores

gender_confidence is returned as text. Convert it before comparing:

d <- parse_names(c("JOHN SMITH", "PAT SMITH", "J SMITH", "CHRIS JONES"))
d$gender_confidence <- as.numeric(d$gender_confidence)
d$gender_80 <- ifelse(d$gender_confidence >= 80, d$gender, "U")
d[c("name", "gender", "gender_confidence", "gender_80")]
#>          name gender gender_confidence gender_80
#> 1  JOHN SMITH      M              99.8         M
#> 2   PAT SMITH      F              59.5         U
#> 3     J SMITH      U              50.0         U
#> 4 CHRIS JONES      M              94.4         M

A threshold of 80 (what nickname_lookup() uses) keeps most names and drops the ones that are close to even. For counts of women and men in a population, summing the shares can be better than counting hard calls, because it does not round every PAT to female.

Keep in mind:

  • The counts are for the whole U.S. population in 2020, children included. Name use changes over time (LESLIE and ASHLEY were once mostly male names; TAYLOR and RILEY have become mostly female) and across countries, so the score fits some groups better than others.
  • The census lists record only male and female. The scores say nothing about how people identify.
  • Names missing from the list, many of them non-English given names, get no score at all.

Where the census table comes from

census.names is bundled with the package in data/census.names.rda. It is not downloaded when the package is installed or used. It is built by data-raw/census_names.R from the Census Bureau’s 2020 name release, Frequently Occurring First Names and Last Names from the 2020 Census (revised April 2026):

cn <- census.names
c(rows           = nrow(cn),
  male_names     = sum(cn$male_value > 0),
  female_names   = sum(cn$female_value > 0),
  first_names    = sum(cn$first_name_value > 0),
  surnames       = sum(cn$last_name_value > 0))
#>         rows   male_names female_names  first_names     surnames 
#>       195311        47089        51475        53616       156622
cn[cn$name %in% c("SMITH", "ALL OTHER NAMES"), ]
#> Key: <name>
#>               name male_value female_value first_name_value last_name_value
#>             <fctr>      <num>        <num>            <num>           <num>
#> 1: ALL OTHER NAMES    7768920     11025786         18794706        36257637
#> 2:           SMITH       4102          897             4999         2369644
  • Given names and gender: every first name held by 91 or more people in the 2020 Census, with the count of people recorded male and female. first_name_value is male_value + female_value.
  • Surnames: every surname held by 92 or more people, plus a catch-all ALL OTHER NAMES row (which no single name token matches).

Earlier table. Until November 2026 the package shipped a table built from the 1990 first-name lists (1,219 male and 4,275 female names, published as percentages and scaled to counts) and the 2010 surname file. The 2020 lists hold ten times as many given names, so far fewer names get no gender. On a sample of 9,608 Form 990 Part VII names, the 2020 table:

  • matched the gender implied by an MR, MRS or MS salutation in 86% of cases, against 79%;
  • left 227 names with unknown gender, against 727;
  • kept the written first word as the first name in 96.3% of plain two- and three-word names, against 95.4%.

Refreshing the table. When the Bureau publishes new lists, update the file names in data-raw/census_names.R and run it from the package root. It downloads the files, records their sizes and SHA-256 hashes in data-raw/census-names-src.csv, rebuilds the five columns, and prints a comparison with the bundled table: size, names whose main role (first name or surname) changes, and names whose majority gender flips. Set CENSUS_NAMES_SAVE=TRUE to overwrite the bundled table, then rerun the tests and compare parses before and after, since any change moves name-order and gender results.
